topics.title: Practical diodes: equation, 0.7 V model, temperature
topics.summary: Real diodes follow the exponential Shockley equation; for quick work use a 0.7 V drop that falls about 2 mV per °C.

lensNotes.circuit: Pick the simplest model that answers the question: ideal (0 V), constant drop (0.7 V for silicon), or the full exponential when currents span decades or temperature matters.
lensNotes.physics: Current grows as e^(V/V_T) because carriers must climb an energy barrier, and the fraction that gets over follows a Boltzmann distribution. That's why V_T = kT/q appears, and why hotter diodes conduct at lower voltage.

prerequisiteNotes.ideal_diode: The 0.7 V and exponential models refine the on/off picture: a real diode needs some forward voltage, and its current grows exponentially with it.

goals: Choose the simplest model that answers the question: ideal switch, constant 0.7 V drop, or the exponential diode equation
Find a diode circuit's current with the 0.7 V model, and a diode's current or voltage from I = I_S(e^(V/(nV_T)) − 1)
Use the 60 mV-per-decade rule (n = 1) to say how far the forward voltage moves when the current changes tenfold
Predict how a silicon diode's forward voltage shifts with temperature (about −2 mV/°C at a fixed current) and explain why
topics.intuition: In a forward-biased silicon diode at room temperature, every extra 60 mV or so multiplies the current by ten (for n = 1), so across the milliamp currents most circuits use, its voltage stays near 0.6–0.7 V.
topics.why: Forward current is carried by carriers with enough thermal energy to get over the junction's barrier. Their number falls exponentially with the barrier's height, so each V_T = kT/q (about 26 mV) of extra forward voltage lets e ≈ 2.7 times as many across when n = 1: I = I_S(e^(V/(nV_T)) − 1), where n is 1 to about 2. Tenfold current needs n·V_T·ln 10, about 60 mV at n = 1. I_S is proportional to n_i², the square of the density of heat-freed carriers, so it roughly doubles every 5 °C, far faster than V_T grows. At a fixed current, the drop therefore falls about 2 mV/°C.
topics.explanation: Unlike the ideal diode, a real silicon diode needs a few tenths of a volt before it passes a useful current. Three models of increasing detail describe it. The ideal model, a short or an open, is good enough when 0.7 V is a small part of the supply. The constant-drop model, a fixed 0.7 V when on, suits most circuit work: I = (V − 0.7 V)/R. The exponential (Shockley) equation, I = I_S(e^(V/(nV_T)) − 1), is the full picture. I_S, the reverse saturation current, is a tiny current set by the junction's size, doping, and temperature; n, the ideality factor, lies between 1 and 2. Use it when the supply is only a volt or two, when currents span decades, or when temperature matters. Two rules come from it. Ten times the current adds about 60 mV at n = 1 (120 mV at n = 2). Warming the diode lowers its drop about 2 mV per °C at a fixed current. In reverse bias, all three models give almost no current. Real diodes leak a little, and beyond the breakdown voltage the current rises sharply, which none of the three models show.

workedExample.problem: A silicon diode, modeled with I_S = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ A and n = 1 at 300 K (V_T = 25.85 mV), is in series with R = 1.0 kΩ across a 5.0 V supply. Find the current with each of the three models, then repeat with a 1.5 V supply. Finally, estimate the diode's voltage at ten times the current, and after warming it by 50 °C.
steps: Ideal model (0 V drop): I = 5.0 V / 1.0 kΩ = 5.00 mA.
Constant-drop model (0.7 V): I = (5.0 V − 0.7 V) / 1.0 kΩ = 4.30 mA.

Exponential model: the diode voltage and the current depend on each other, so iterate (the −1 is negligible when I is so far above I_S). Start from 4.30 mA: V_D = n·V_T·ln(I/I_S) = 25.85 mV × ln(4.30 mA / 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ A) = 25.85 mV × 24.48 = 0.633 V. Then I = (5.0 V − 0.633 V) / 1.0 kΩ = 4.37 mA. Repeating at 4.37 mA gives V_D = 25.85 mV × 24.50 = 0.633 V again, so I = 4.37 mA.
Compare at 5 V: the 0.7 V model (4.30 mA) is 1.6% low and the ideal model (5.00 mA) is 14% high. Here the 0.7 V model is good enough.

At 1.5 V. Ideal: 1.5 V / 1.0 kΩ = 1.50 mA. Constant drop: (1.5 V − 0.7 V) / 1.0 kΩ = 0.80 mA. Exponential: from 0.80 mA, V_D = 25.85 mV × ln(0.80 mA / 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ A) = 25.85 mV × 22.80 = 0.589 V, so I = (1.5 V − 0.589 V) / 1.0 kΩ = 0.911 mA. Again: V_D = 25.85 mV × ln(0.911 mA / 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ A) = 25.85 mV × 22.93 = 0.593 V, so I = 0.907 mA, where it settles.
Compare at 1.5 V: the 0.7 V model is now 12% low and the ideal model 65% high. With only a volt or two of supply, the diode's exact drop matters, and only the exponential model will do.

Ten times the current (exponential model, n = 1): V_D rises by V_T·ln 10 = 25.85 mV × 2.303 = 59.5 mV, so at 43.7 mA (with a smaller resistor or a larger supply) the diode drops about 0.633 V + 0.060 V = 0.693 V. A real diode drops a little more at tens of milliamps, across the resistance of its silicon and leads, which the equation leaves out.

Temperature (rule of thumb, −2 mV/°C at a fixed current): At 50 °C warmer, V_D ≈ 0.633 V − 2 mV/°C × 50 °C = 0.533 V. In the 5.0 V circuit, the current rises only to about (5.0 V − 0.533 V) / 1.0 kΩ = 4.47 mA, 2% more: the drop moved by 100 mV, but the resistor, with over 4 V across it, still sets the current. The 2% rise in current puts back only V_T·ln 1.02 ≈ 0.5 mV, so treating the current as fixed was fair.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 3 "Diodes and Rectifiers", section "Introduction"
sources.note: The diode equation I = I_S(e^(V/(nV_T)) − 1) with V_T = kT/q of about 26 mV at room temperature and an ideality factor of 1 to 2, the constant 0.7 V drop as the usual simplification because the drop changes little over a wide current range, and small reverse leakage up to breakdown.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "PN Junctions and Diodes", ch. 2 "Tutorial", section 2.3 "PN junction diode behavior"
sources.note: The Shockley equation with n = 1 for a perfect junction, I_S as a tiny reverse saturation current that changes strongly with temperature, a forward drop that falls as the junction warms, and simulated currents at 0.6 V and 0.7 V that work out to about 60 mV per decade.

templates.prompt: Using the constant-voltage-drop model (0.7 V), how much current flows when a {V} source drives a silicon diode and a {R} resistor in series?
templates.explanation: The diode takes 0.7 V, leaving {VR} across the resistor: I = {VR} / {R} = {answer}.
hints: Subtract the diode drop before applying Ohm's law.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the diode's 0.7 V drop (the ideal model). Subtract it first: I = (V − 0.7) / R.
The diode drops voltage, so subtract 0.7 V.

followUps.prompt: The model uses 0.7 V for the diode whatever the current. Why is that fair?

choices.text: The diode's current grows exponentially with its voltage, so even ten times the current raises the drop by only about 60 mV (n = 1; about 120 mV for n = 2)
choices.feedback: Right: V = V_T·ln(I/I_S), and a logarithm barely moves. Currents from 0.1 mA to 100 mA all fit within about 0.5–0.8 V.

choices.text: The diode contains a fixed 0.7 V barrier that acts like a small battery
choices.feedback: A battery could push current around the loop by itself; a diode never does. The barrier is lowered by the applied voltage, and how far it is lowered sets the current exponentially.

choices.text: The series resistor holds the diode's voltage at 0.7 V
choices.feedback: The resistor sets the current, through Ohm's law on the voltage left over. The diode's own exponential law is what keeps its voltage near 0.7 V.

choices.text: The diode's drop grows in proportion to the current, but the current here hardly varies
choices.feedback: If the drop were proportional to current, the diode would be a resistor. Across these problems the current varies more than tenfold, yet the drop stays near 0.7 V.

followUps.explanation: From the Shockley equation, V_D = V_T·ln(I/I_S): each tenfold rise in current adds only V_T·ln 10 ≈ 60 mV. So once a silicon diode conducts a useful current, its voltage sits in a narrow band around 0.6–0.7 V, and a fixed 0.7 V is a good stand-in. Kirchhoff's voltage law then leaves V − 0.7 V for the resistor, and Ohm's law gives the current.

templates.prompt: A diode has saturation current I_S = {Is} and ideality factor n = 1, at a thermal voltage of 25.85 mV. What current flows with {Vd} across it?
templates.explanation: Shockley: I = I_S (e^(V/(nV_T)) − 1) = {Is} × (e^({Vd}/25.85 mV) − 1) = {answer}. The exponential is why the voltage hardly changes over a wide range of currents.
hints: Compute V/V_T first; the −1 hardly matters in forward bias.

misconceptions.feedback: Divide the voltage by the thermal voltage inside the exponent: e^(V / V_T).

templates.noDrawing: the Shockley equation for one diode, no circuit
templates.formulaStepsWhy: One relation: the Shockley equation, I = I_S(e^(V/V_T) − 1).

templates.prompt: A diode with I_S = {Is} and n = 1 carries {I} at a thermal voltage of 25.85 mV. What is its forward voltage?
templates.explanation: Invert the Shockley equation: V = n·V_T·ln(I/I_S + 1) = 25.85 mV × ln({I} / {Is} + 1) = {answer}.

misconceptions.feedback: Use the natural log (ln), not log₁₀: the exponential is base e.

templates.noDrawing: the Shockley equation for one diode, no circuit
templates.formulaStepsWhy: One relation: the Shockley equation solved for V, V = V_T·ln(I/I_S + 1).

templates.prompt: A diode's current rises by a factor of {k} (n = 1, V_T = 25.85 mV). By how much does its forward voltage rise?
templates.explanation: Taking the ratio of two Shockley equations: ΔV = n·V_T·ln(I₂/I₁), and with n = 1 that is 25.85 mV × ln({k}) = {answer}. For a factor of 10, that's about 60 mV: the famous "60 mV per decade."
hints: Write V = V_T ln(I/I_S) for both currents and subtract.

misconceptions.feedback: That assumes the diode voltage grows in proportion to the current. It grows only logarithmically: ΔV = V_T · ln(ratio).
The exponential is base e, so use ln: ΔV = V_T·ln(ratio) = 2.303·V_T·log₁₀(ratio), about 60 mV per decade, not 26 mV.

templates.noDrawing: the Shockley equation for one diode, no circuit

templates.prompt: A silicon diode carrying a fixed current drops {Vf} at 25 °C. Using a temperature coefficient of −2 mV/°C, what is its forward voltage at {T2}?
templates.explanation: ΔT = {dT}. The forward voltage changes by −2 mV/°C × {dT}, so V = {Vf} − 0.002 × ({dT}) = {answer}. Hotter diodes drop less voltage, which is why diodes make simple temperature sensors.
hints: V = V_f − 2 mV/°C × ΔT: hotter means lower voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: The coefficient is negative: the forward voltage falls as temperature rises.

followUps.prompt: At a fixed current, why does a hotter diode need less forward voltage?

choices.text: Heat gives more carriers enough energy to get over the barrier (I_S rises steeply), so the barrier needn't be pulled down as far: less forward voltage passes the same current
choices.feedback: Right: I_S roughly doubles every 5 °C or so. In V = V_T·ln(I/I_S) that wins over the slow rise of V_T, and V falls about 2 mV/°C.

choices.text: The thermal voltage V_T = kT/q rises with temperature, which lowers the drop
choices.feedback: V_T rising on its own would raise V = V_T·ln(I/I_S), not lower it. The drop falls because I_S rises much faster than V_T.

choices.text: Silicon's resistance rises with temperature, so the diode needs less voltage
choices.feedback: A higher resistance would need more voltage for the same current, not less. The effect comes from the junction's barrier, not from a resistance.

choices.text: The diode's leakage current rises and bypasses the junction
choices.feedback: Leakage is nanoamps against milliamps of forward current; the drop falls because I_S rises steeply.

followUps.explanation: V_F = V_T·ln(I/I_S). Warming the diode makes many more thermally generated carriers, and I_S goes as n_i², the square of their density, so I_S climbs steeply, far faster than V_T = kT/q. At the same current the ratio I/I_S shrinks, and V_F drops by about 2 mV per °C. This is the thermal voltage from the PN junction topic at work.

templates.noDrawing: one diode's temperature coefficient, no circuit

templates.prompt: Why can a silicon diode carrying a constant forward current be used as a thermometer?

choices.text: Its forward voltage falls about 2 mV per °C, because hotter carriers cross the junction more easily
choices.feedback: Yes: the Shockley equation's I_S rises steeply with temperature, so less voltage gives the same current.

choices.text: Its resistance rises with temperature like a metal wire
choices.feedback: A diode's voltage actually falls with temperature, the opposite of a metal's resistance.

choices.text: Its current rises with temperature, which the meter reads
choices.feedback: The circuit holds the current constant; what changes is the voltage needed to pass it.

Breakdown needs a reverse voltage beyond the rating, and its temperature coefficient depends on the mechanism (negative below about 5 V, positive above); a forward-biased silicon junction at a fixed current gives about −2 mV/°C in any diode.

templates.explanation: At a fixed current, V_F ≈ V_T·ln(I/I_S). I_S grows very fast with temperature (more thermally generated carriers), which outweighs V_T's slow rise, so V_F drops by about 2 mV/°C: a clean, nearly linear sensor.

templates.prompt: A silicon diode with I_S = {Is} (n = 1, room temperature, V_T = 25.85 mV) is fed from {Vs} through a series resistor. Choose R (an E24 value, 100 Ω to 100 kΩ) so the diode current is {I} within 5%. The simulator checks your design with the full diode equation.

sim.note: The 0.7 V model is too rough here: at {I} this diode drops only about {Vd}, and with just {Vs} of supply that difference changes the current a lot. Use V_D = V_T·ln(I/I_S).

templates.explanation: From the diode equation, V_D = V_T·ln(I/I_S) = 25.85 mV × ln({I} / {Is}) = {Vd}. Then R = ({Vs} − V_D)/I = {Rex}; pick the nearest E24 value. The 0.7 V model would give {Rcv}, which lets too much current flow because the real drop is lower.
hints: With a supply this small, a 0.1 V error in the diode drop matters.

templates.prompt: A silicon diode (I_S = {Is}, n = 1, room temperature, V_T = 25.85 mV) has {Vd} across it. The voltage is raised to {new_Vd}, just 60 mV more. What happens to the current through it?

whatIf.factorHint: The current isn't a power of the voltage: it goes as e^(V/V_T), so a step ΔV multiplies it by e^(ΔV/V_T), whatever voltage you start from. Work out ΔV/V_T for 60 mV.

feedback.down: More forward voltage lowers the junction's barrier further, so more carriers have the energy to get over it.
feedback.same: 60 mV looks small next to {Vd}, but the forward voltage lowers the junction's barrier, and the number of carriers with enough energy to cross it grows exponentially as the barrier falls: I follows e^(V/V_T), with V_T about 26 mV.

templates.explanation: Shockley: I = I_S(e^(V/V_T) − 1). Raising V by ΔV multiplies the current by e^(ΔV/V_T) = e^(0.06/0.02585) ≈ 10: {before} → {after}. Read the other way, that's the "60 mV per decade" rule: ten times the current costs only about 60 mV more. It is why a conducting diode's voltage barely changes with current, and why you should never connect a diode straight across a supply: a little too much voltage means far too much current.
hints: The current depends on e^(V/V_T), not on V in proportion.

followUps.prompt: A classmate says 660 mV is only 10% more than 600 mV, so the current rises about 10%. What's wrong?

choices.text: The current depends on e^(V/V_T), so what matters is the 60 mV step compared with V_T ≈ 26 mV, not compared with 600 mV: e^(60/25.85) ≈ 10.
choices.feedback: Right: in an exponential, equal steps in voltage multiply the current by equal factors. 60 mV is about 2.3 V_T, and e^2.3 ≈ 10, whatever voltage you start from.

choices.text: Nothing: a diode obeys Ohm's law once it conducts, so 10% more voltage gives 10% more current.
choices.feedback: A diode never follows Ohm's law. If it did, its voltage would rise in proportion to its current; instead, a conducting diode stays near 0.6–0.7 V while its current changes a thousandfold.

choices.text: The current rises by 60 mV/V_T ≈ 2.3 times, in proportion to the step measured in V_T.
choices.feedback: 2.3 is the exponent, not the factor. The current goes as e^(V/V_T): every V_T of extra voltage multiplies it by e ≈ 2.7, so a step of 2.3 V_T multiplies it by e^2.3.

followUps.explanation: Shockley's law, I = I_S(e^(V/V_T) − 1), is exponential: a step ΔV multiplies the current by e^(ΔV/V_T), however large V already is. So the size of the step is judged against V_T ≈ 26 mV, the thermal voltage, not against the 600 mV already there. 60 mV is about 2.3 V_T, and e^2.3 ≈ 10: the "60 mV per decade" rule.

templates.prompt: A {V} battery drives a silicon diode and a resistor R = {R} in series (use the 0.7 V model). A second, identical battery is added in series, so the supply is now {new_V}. What happens to the current?

whatIf.factorHint: The current is the resistor's voltage over R, (V − 0.7 V)/R, and the diode's 0.7 V stays put: compare V − 0.7 V with 2V − 0.7 V. It's a fixed drop, not a square or a root.

feedback.down: The diode still drops about 0.7 V, so the extra supply voltage all lands on the resistor, and more voltage across the same resistor means more current.
feedback.same: The diode holds its own voltage near 0.7 V; it doesn't hold the current. The resistor takes everything else, so all of the added battery voltage lands across it, and I = (V − 0.7 V)/R.

templates.explanation: By Kirchhoff's voltage law, the resistor gets V − 0.7 V, and by Ohm's law I = (V − 0.7 V)/R: {before} → {after}. The current more than doubles, because doubling V more than doubles V − 0.7 V: the diode's share stays at 0.7 V while all the extra goes to the resistor. The current in a plain resistor circuit would exactly double; the diode's fixed drop breaks the proportion, most of all at low supply voltages.
hints: What voltage does the resistor get before and after?

templates.prompt: A {V} supply lights an LED (D2) through resistor R1 = {R} and a protection diode D1, which blocks current if the supply is ever connected backward (an LED survives only about 5 V in reverse). When the circuit is healthy, the meters should read {h0} at node b (D1's cathode), {h1} at node c (the LED's anode), and {h2} through R1. The readings are below. Which fault explains them?

fault.netlist:
LED with protection diode
V1 a 0 {V:spice}
D1 a b DN
R1 b c {R:spice}
D2 c 0 DL
.model DN D
.model DL D(IS=1e-18 N=2)

probes.label: Voltage at node c (the LED's anode)

faults.feedback: An open D1 would cut the whole chain off from the supply: no current, and node b would fall to about 0 V instead of sitting near the supply.
faults.why: No current flows and nothing connects b to the supply anymore, so b and c both read about 0 V ({m0}): the break is before b.

faults.feedback: A shorted D1 would put b at the full {V} and let a little more current flow (the 0.7 V it used to take now goes to R1), with the LED still lit.
faults.why: Node b reads the full supply, {m0}, instead of about 0.7 V below it. The resistor now gets 0.7 V more, so the current rises a little, to {m2}. The LED still works, but the circuit has lost its protection.

faults.feedback: An open R1 would stop the current. With no current, D1 would drop only a few tenths of a volt, so b would rise close to the supply, while c, past the break, would read about 0 V.
faults.why: No current flows, so D1 drops only a few tenths of a volt: b reads {m0}, close to the supply. Past the break, c reads about 0 V ({m1}). The voltage jumps across R1 with no current through it, so R1 is the break.

faults.feedback: An open LED would stop the current, and with no current neither D1 nor R1 would drop much, so both b and c would read close to the supply.
faults.why: No current flows, and both b ({m0}) and c ({m1}) sit near the supply. Without current, a resistor drops nothing and a diode drops only a few tenths of a volt, so the break is at the LED.

faults.feedback: A shorted LED would pull c to 0 V and let more current flow, because R1 then gets the LED's {h1} as well.
faults.why: Node c reads 0 V, so c is tied to ground. The current rises to {m2} because R1 now gets everything but D1's 0.7 V.

templates.explanation: Follow the current first: zero means something in the chain is open; more than normal means something is shorted. Then use the node voltages. With no current, a resistor drops nothing and a diode only a few tenths of a volt (Ohm's law, and the diode equation at a tiny current), so the voltage stays high up to the break and reads about 0 V after it. A short shows up as two points that read the same voltage.
hints: Is the current zero, normal, or higher than normal?
With no current, where does the voltage jump from high to low?
